title: Entrepreneurial Actions and Succession Planning among Small and Medium Family-Owned Businesses in Uganda
affiliations: Mountains of the Moon University, Makerere University Business School, Makerere University - Business School, Makerere University Business School and

detail.title: Entrepreneurial Actions and Succession Planning among Small and Medium Family-Owned Businesses in Uganda
detail.abstract: PurposeThis study explored the synergistic relationship between entrepreneurial actions and succession planning as drivers of sustainability in family enterprises across generations in Uganda.MethodologyThe study used a cross-sectional research design with a quantitative approach. Data were collected via questionnaires from 230 family business owners, identified through a snowball sampling technique. The data were analyzed using SMART PLS.FindingsThe findings revealed that dynamic capabilities and opportunity identification are positively and significantly related to succession planning, while innovation showed no significant relationship with succession planning in small and medium family-owned businesses in Uganda.Research limitationsThe study employed a cross-sectional study and was limited to small and medium enterprises. With the availability of resources, a longitudinal study can be conducted covering large family enterprises.Practical implicationFamily business owners can leverage the entrepreneurial ecosystem for opportunity identification and dynamic capabilities to enhance succession planning. Additionally, innovation should be embedded in the broader ecosystem, which provides financing, mentorship and regulatory support for family business continuity.Originality/ValueIntegrating entrepreneurial actions like dynamic capabilities and opportunity identification into succession planning is most likely to strengthen family businesses for generations.

title: Digital Leadership as a Strategic Response: How Innovation Capabilities Mediate Global Competitiveness in a Constrained Emerging Economy

detail.title: Digital Leadership as a Strategic Response: How Innovation Capabilities Mediate Global Competitiveness in a Constrained Emerging Economy
detail.abstract: This research focuses on studying the role of digital leadership in global competitiveness by shaping innovation capabilities in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) organizations in a constrained emerging economy. Grounded in the Resource-Based View (RBV) and the Dynamic Capabilities (DC) perspective, it explores five dimensions of digital leadership: inspirational, innovative, uncertainty management, adaptive, and visionary and how these influence competitive advantage. A quantitative and cross-sectional survey among 204 C-level executives working in ICT firms was analyzed with the help of PLS-SEM. The results show that all leadership dimensions have a significant impact on enhancing the innovation capabilities while the innovative and uncertainty management roles have a direct impact as well on the competitive advantage. Critically, innovation capabilities show a strong positive relationship with competitive advantage and fully mediate the effect of leadership dimensions in confirming their role as the central mechanism through that digital leadership translates into sustained global positioning in the markets. The findings provide theoretical understanding of leadership as a higher-order dynamic capability and practical advice for firms managing digital transformation in institutionally complex settings.

title: From Strategy to Execution: A Capability System Perspective for Business Model Design and Transformation
affiliations: LUT University

detail.title: From Strategy to Execution: A Capability System Perspective for Business Model Design and Transformation
detail.abstract: Abstract. We introduce the Business Required Capabilities (BRC) framework for business model design and execution in dynamic contexts and illustrate its use in a real-world business transformation setting. The framework conceptualizes business models as three interdependent elements: Customer Value Proposition, a multi-level Capability System, and Financial System and Risk Exposure—anchored in strategy and linked by two Coordination Technologies: Value Configuration Technology for intra-capability orchestration and Value Interaction Technology for cross-capability interaction. Renewal is positioned as a fourth business model function, grounded in contextual ambidexterity—reframed as a systemic capability-system quality that links internal alignment, renewal, and external shaping—and in strategic capability prepositioning, which embeds option-like capacity. Value configuration and value interaction technologies reinforce the execution and open strategic options. An equilibrium lens and a routinization continuum further connect design to performance. KONE corporation’s digital transformation illustrates how the framework operationalizes the resource-based view of the firm and dynamic-capabilities foundations. Managerially, the framework provides a concise diagnostic to guide need- and outcome-based innovation and business-model transformation.

title: Measuring Educational Friction: A Dual-Tension Framework for Ontario's Funding & Governance Landscape

detail.title: Measuring Educational Friction: A Dual-Tension Framework for Ontario's Funding & Governance Landscape

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no financial or personal conflicts of interest related to the development of this research. The conceptual and analytical framework was independently developed by the author, and no external party influenced the research design, interpretation, or conclusions
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available documents and theoretical modeling only. No human participants or private data were involved, and formal ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was fully self-supported by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper presents a structural framework for examining educational funding tension in Ontario using Fiscal Geometry, a two-axis model that maps fiscal movement across jurisdictions (X-axis) and intergenerational post-tax capacity (Y-axis). Rather than evaluating policy outcomes or prescribing solutions, the paper proposes a visibility-first approach: treating public administrative rules and funding formulas as events that generate measurable patterns within a coordinate space. Building on previous work on the Institutional Tension Index (ITI) and the extended dual index development of ETI (Emotional Tension Index) and EPTI (Educational Performance Tension Index), this paper outlines how a dual-tension geometry can function as a diagnostic system for detecting stagnation signals such as EQAO plateaus, allocation bottlenecks, and governance friction.

title: Gatekeeper of Rights V: Supranational Memory and Domestic Amnesia in Hungarian Rights Protections
affiliations: Semmelweis University

detail.title: Gatekeeper of Rights V: Supranational Memory and Domestic Amnesia in Hungarian Rights Protections

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the complainant and affected student in the underlying Semmelweis University case examined in this article. All factual descriptions of events, correspondence, and procedures are based on primary documents, court and authority filings, and institutional communications available to the author; where possible, these are cited or appended. The author has no financial interest in any outcome arising from this publication. The purpose of the article is to document, analyse, and contextualise the operation of domestic and supranational rights-protection mechanisms in higher education, not to seek individual compensation or a change in his personal academic status.

keywords: Article 41 CFR's Right to Good Adminstration
Article X of Hungarian Fundamental Law

detail.abstract:
In November 2025, the European Parliament adopted its second interim report on Hungary under Article 7(1) TEU (415–193–28), reiterating its classification as a “hybrid regime of electoral autocracy” and calling for tougher use of conditionality and budgetary tools. At the same time, Council Decision (EU) 2022/2506 and a revised RRF/Repower EU plan have left most of Hungary’s EU funding effectively frozen behind twenty-seven “super-milestones” on judicial independence, anti-corruption, and academic-freedom safeguards. This article argues that, against this backdrop, Hungary’s higher-education sector now operates within a split memory regime: while supranational institutions diligently record structural rule-of-law failures, domestic watchdogs and quality-assurance actors increasingly cultivate domestic amnesia.

Using a detailed case study from Semmelweis University’s English-language medical program—denial of access to compulsory dissection, an unsecured “Survey About Academic Progress”, coerced OMHV questionnaire participation through priority exam registration, and a dean-level takedown threat against whistleblower publications—the article reconstructs how the Commissioner for Fundamental Rights (AJBH), the Equal Treatment unit, NAIH, and MAB generate file numbers but avoid merit-based decisions. The resulting Ombudsman–court deflection loop produces an illusory remedy: institutions exist and “coordinate” under Ebktv. 15/B and Ark. 48, yet nobody adjudicates the substance of the rights claims.

Doctrinally, the article reads this configuration as a breach of Article 41 CFR’s right to good administration, Article 47 CFR’s right to an effective remedy, Article 13 CFR, and Article X of the Hungarian Fundamental Law on academic freedom. It concludes that supranational memory and budget conditionality have become the Union’s only reliable levers for protecting student and educational rights in Hungary. It suggests indicators for integrating domestic archiving practices and institutional silence into the EU’s 2026 Rule of Law cycle.

title: Long-term evolution of pH and metals (Al, Fe, Mn, U) in pyrite-bearing waste rocks using reactive transport modeling: dealing with stock and process uncertainties
affiliations: Université Paris-Dauphine, PSL Research University - MINES ParisTech, Université Paris Est Créteil - Sorbonne Université, Consultant, Mines Paris - PSL, , , Mines Paris - PSL, ,  and

detail.title: Long-term evolution of pH and metals (Al, Fe, Mn, U) in pyrite-bearing waste rocks using reactive transport modeling: dealing with stock and process uncertainties
detail.abstract: Hydrogeochemical management of mine effluents is essential to ensure a responsible and sustainable mining industry. These effluents can be heavily affected by acid mine drainage (AMD) over time spans that often extend over decades, during which continuous monitoring and treatment are required. However, significant uncertainties typically remain regarding the duration and evolution of AMD, as the source terms are often poorly characterized particularly in the case of old or legacy mines. For mining operators, reducing these uncertainties represents a key advantage for optimizing long-term treatment and operational strategies, both technically and economically. In this study, we use reactive transport (RT) modeling to interpret 30 years of monitoring data from the former Bertholène uranium mine in France. Our results show that metal loadings have steadily decreased, for some of them, to levels below regulatory limits, in parallel with a general decline in sulfide oxidation rates. This improved understanding will contribute to the development of a treatment strategy. In the coming decades, treatment will focus on addressing the remaining acidity, rather than on metals or radionuclides whose pre-treatment concentrations should comply with regulatory requirements.

title: Towards transferable models of cyclist route choice: a mode-constrained mixture approach
affiliations: ,  and

detail.title: Towards transferable models of cyclist route choice: a mode-constrained mixture approach
detail.abstract: Cities increasingly rely on bike-sharing systems to promote sustainable mobility. These systems generate massive but low-granularity data. Unlike GPS datasets, trip records typically provide only the origin, destination and total duration, making it difficult to infer route structure or behavioral heterogeneity. Despite this limited granularity, some studies have shown that trip-duration distributions are usually well represented by a mixture of log-normal distributions, with a strong linear relationship between the first component mode and the theoretical fastest duration provided by OpenStreetMap. To exploit this relationship, we propose a mode-constrained mixture model, in which the mode of the first component is linearly linked to the theoretical travel time. This approach is validated on the 2.4 million trips recorded in HelsinkiEspoo in 2024, which has the particularity of including both durations and distances. On these data, the lesser variability of distances makes it much easier to identify the groups of the mixture model. The estimated group proportions are then confronted to those estimated from the durations as a way to validate the method. This transferable method offers urban planners a reliable tool to infer route choice without GPS data, supporting the design of cycling infrastructure and the modeling of travel demand.

title: When Do Digital Transformation Capabilities Pay Off? Evidence from Innovation Efficiency and Board Technology Expertise in an Emerging Economy
affiliations: Andhra University, Andhra University, ,  and Andhra University

detail.title: When Do Digital Transformation Capabilities Pay Off? Evidence from Innovation Efficiency and Board Technology Expertise in an Emerging Economy
detail.abstract: This study examines when digital transformation capabilities translate into superior financial performance. Using survey data from 493 senior executives of Indian firms, we show that digital transformation capabilities enhance financial performance primarily through innovation efficiency, highlighting innovation productivity as the central mechanism of digital value creation. By identifying innovation efficiency as the key transmission channel, the study extends entrepreneurship and innovation research on digital value creation. Contrary to conventional expectations, board technological competence weakens the direct financial impact of digital transformation, indicating that technologically sophisticated boards may adopt more cautious governance and investment approaches that delay short-term financial payoffs. These finding challenges prevailing assumptions in governance theory by positioning board technological competence as a boundary condition rather than a uniformly positive moderator. From a managerial perspective, the results suggest that firms should complement digital investments with practices that accelerate innovation execution, while boards need to balance technological expertise with strategic agility to avoid postponing the financial benefits of digital transformation in emerging economies.

title: SPATIOTEMPORAL ANALYSIS OF LAND USE/COVER CHANGE AND ITS DRIVING FACTOR IN THE GAMBELLA ZURIE WOREDA, GAMBELLA REGION, ETHIOPIA
affiliations: Gambella University, Gambella University and Gambella University

detail.title: SPATIOTEMPORAL ANALYSIS OF LAND USE/COVER CHANGE AND ITS DRIVING FACTOR IN THE GAMBELLA ZURIE WOREDA, GAMBELLA REGION, ETHIOPIA
detail.abstract: This study aims to assess spatial-temporal analysis of  land use land cover dynamics and its driving factors in Gambella woreda, Gambella region, southwest Ethiopia over a period of 20 years (2003–2023). Satellite images of Landsat TM (2003), ETM+ (2013), and OIL/TIRS (2023) were used. A total of 200 questionnaires were collected from household heads in the four Kebelle. A data was analysis and presented using ARCGIS 10.8, ERDAS Imagine version 2015, and Binary logistic regression. Six LULCs were successfully captured with overall accuracies ranging from 86% to 90% and Kappa statistic of 0.83 to 0.87. The findings showed that, the most dominant increase from 2003 to 2023 was observed in cropland, which expanded from 9.4% in 2003 to 25.9% in 2023, followed by wooded grassland (22.7% to 21.14%) and settlements (7.9% to 10.95%). Conversely, forest cover experienced the most significant decline, decreasing from 32.2% to 15%, while water bodies and scrubland also declined from 12.6% to 15.52% and 15.3% to 11.5%, respectively. And LULC mainly driven by population growth, expanding agricultural activities, increasing demand for fuel wood and construction materials, and the lack of effective natural resource conservation policies. They also show that education and occupation shape perceptions of land use change; individuals with higher levels of education are more likely to recognize these changes (OR = 2.30), while farmers have a greater tendency (OR = 1.75) to link land transformation to agricultural expansion. The study recommends further research to investigate the specific drivers and associated impacts of these changes.

title: Innovative Small and Medium Industrial Clusters, Urban-Rural Income and Inequality
affiliations: , Beihang University (BUAA) - School of Economic and Management Science and Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) - Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science (AMSS)

detail.title: Innovative Small and Medium Industrial Clusters, Urban-Rural Income and Inequality
detail.abstract: Small-medium industry clusters (SMICs) represent the latest development of national high-quality development program in China. They concentrate in county-level regions and emphasize specialization, refinement, and innovation. This paper links clusters and residents’ income, studies the impact of SMICs on urban- rural income and inequality. We find that SMICs significantly increase urban-rural income. Mechanism analysis shows that SMICs raise income through enhancing employment rates, innovation drive and multiplier effect on industry integration development. SMICs generate strong demand for skilled labor and promote rapid intra-cluster knowledge diffusion. As for the urban-rural inequality, only SMICs that fully integrated with the local economy making best use of local resource advantages can effectively reduce the urban-rural income inequality.

title: Exploring Psychological and Contextual Factors Influencing Informal Mid-Block Pedestrian Crossings in LMICs: Evidence from Dhaka
affiliations: University of Asia Pacific, University of British Columbia Okanagan, University of Asia Pacific, University of Asia Pacific and University of Asia Pacific

detail.title: Exploring Psychological and Contextual Factors Influencing Informal Mid-Block Pedestrian Crossings in LMICs: Evidence from Dhaka
detail.abstract: Pedestrians face high risks while crossing roads due to inadequate infrastructure, and in some cases, overconfidence in their own judgment. This study explores the factors influencing pedestrian mid-block crossing behaviors, an area still underexplored in low- and middle-income countries like Bangladesh. Two scenarios were created: one assessed urgent crossing under time pressure and traffic gaps despite available facilities, and the other examined future intentions. A total of 426 responses were collected through a questionnaire survey. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identified six factors: optimal path crossing, enhanced safety perception, careless crossing, crossing triggers, perceived safety, and crossing propensity. A multivariate ordered probit model was employed to identify influencing factors, considering both time pressure behaviour and future intentions. Findings revealed that older individuals, students, public transit, and active transport users are primarily involved in urgent mid-block crossing. A gendered pattern also emerged: females from higher-income households are more involved in urgent crossing than females from lower-income households. Urgent crossing behaviour positively predicts similar future intentions, indicating current risks influence future actions. Furthermore, path analysis was used to investigate direct and indirect relationships among the latent constructs. Output revealed that social and environmental factors promoting careless crossings lowered perceived safety, raising demand for improved infrastructure. Moreover, frequent walking for leisure or health was linked to lower perceived safety, underscoring the scarcity of dedicated pedestrian spaces in Dhaka and comparable LMICs. The study advises policymakers that road safety interventions should complement infrastructure improvements with strategies targeting behaviours, perceptions, and intentions to sustain pedestrian compliance.

title: Impact of Corporate Governance on Family Business in India - A Literature Review
affiliations: and

detail.title: Impact of Corporate Governance on Family Business in India - A Literature Review
detail.abstract: A family business is a commercial organization owned, managed, and controlled by members of a single family, often spanning several generations. The family's influence extends to decision-making, ownership, Governance, and the overall strategic direction of the enterprise, with mutual trust, shared values, and transparency playing critical roles in its functioning.This paper provides a systematic review of the existing literature on the impact of Governance on family businesses. The review highlights the dual dimensions of Governance in family firms: the family dimension and the business dimension and emphasizes the need to distinguish between them when analyzing governance outcomes. The study uncovers persistent gaps and drawbacks in family business governance, such as over-concentration of power, limited transparency, and potential conflicts of interest, which weaken formal governance mechanisms.The paper further contributes by developing a conceptual framework linking antecedents of family involvement with governance structures, and in turn connecting these structures to business and family-level outcomes. The 4 Cs and Family Business landscapes and other reviews argue that while family businesses can strengthen Governance through commitment, legacy, and stewardship values, governance effectiveness ultimately depends on managing family influence in a transparent, professional, and inclusive manner. The paper concludes by outlining future research directions to examine heterogeneity across family firms, the role of generational shifts, and the effectiveness of hybrid governance models.

title: Carrots and Sticks as Dual Insurance for Corporate Green Innovation? Heterogeneity between Multinationals and Local Firms
affiliations: , Peking University and National University of Singapore (NUS) - Sustainable & Green Finance Institute (SGFIN)

detail.title: Carrots and Sticks as Dual Insurance for Corporate Green Innovation? Heterogeneity between Multinationals and Local Firms
detail.abstract: Do government rewards and threats serve as dual insurance to spur corporate green innovation? A common assumption is that such rewards and threats, when combined, could generate additive effects on corporate green innovation. Our study introduces the idea that the joint influence of rewards and threats may depend crucially on how they align with the external demands firms face. We argue that multinational enterprises (MNEs), owing to the diverse pressures arising from their global and local operating environments, may struggle to navigate policy mix in a local jurisdiction, which could lead to a substitutive relationship between rewards and threats in promoting green innovation. In contrast, local firms, whose operating pressures tend to be more unified within the single jurisdiction, may experience complementarity between rewards and threats in promoting green innovation. Leveraging the staggered implementation of environmental protection subsidies (i.e., rewards) and environmental protection inspections (i.e., threats) in China, our panel data analysis provides support for our arguments. Additional analyses reveal that the substitutive effect for MNEs is amplified under conditions when international investor exposure or media attention is high. These findings highlight not only the promise but also the limits of using policy mix (rewards and threats) to foster green innovation among different types of firms.

title: Yield Curve Control and Market Policy Expectations: Evidence from Japan
affiliations: George Washington University

detail.title: Yield Curve Control and Market Policy Expectations: Evidence from Japan
detail.abstract: I examine how a fixed-rate purchase policy, or the yield curve control (YCC), performs better than traditional fixed-quantity QE projects in managing market expectations using evidence from Japan. Japan has the longest history of implementing this novel policy. Using the high-frequency identification method, I captured the monetary policy surprises around the Bank of Japan’s policy meetings in the past two decades. I implemented a customized Bayesian vector autoregression model and decomposed the raw surprises into policy specific and macroeconomic information elements via sign restrictions. My analysis on the decomposed policy surprises shows that YCC reduces market uncertainty and aligns market policy expectations, especially when the control band is sufficiently narrow. This effect extends from the targeted asset, 10-year Japanese government bond, to the shorter end of the yield curve and to other adjacent asset markets, albeit with diminishing magnitude, depending on their distance from the targeted asset in terms of both maturity and asset type. The effect weakens and uncertainty increases as the control band widens. The effect is monetary specific. It doesn’t affect market’s expectation on macroeconomic conditions. My findings suggest that YCC has the potential to be a viable policy option, with the set up of target control band being a crucial consideration in policy design.

title: The Right to Freedom of Thought and the Prohibition of Torture and Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment: Examining the Relationship in the Case of the Coercive and Interrogational Use of Neurotechnology
affiliations: Middlesex University, London

detail.title: The Right to Freedom of Thought and the Prohibition of Torture and Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment: Examining the Relationship in the Case of the Coercive and Interrogational Use of Neurotechnology

keywords: The Right to Freedom of Thought
The Prohibition of Torture and Cruel
Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment

detail.abstract:
The forum internum is a legal concept mainly developed in relation to the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion. It refers to a person’s inner realm, ‘where mental faculties are developed, exercised and defined’. This chapter aims to tease out the prohibition of torture’s protection of the forum internum with reference to case law from the European Court of Human Rights, the United Nations Human Rights Committee, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. By reviewing jurisprudential developments and recent academic scholarship re-orienting the threshold of torture away from the severity of suffering towards the severity of conduct, this chapter identifies ways in which we can approach the question of whether and, if so, when and why the involuntary extraction of information from the mind of a suspect or detainee would amount to a violation of either or both of the right to freedom of thought and the prohibition against torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment (CIDTP). This question places certain conceptions of the prohibition of torture under strain given, for example, that human rights law in part prohibits torture or CIDTP because of the unlawful levels of pain and suffering that are inflicted. Thus, the law on the prohibition of torture ‘assumes that the interrogator will attempt to overcome the detainee’s will with pain’. But does this liberate the pain-free but coerced interrogational use of neurotechnology from the definitional bounds of the prohibition of torture or ill-treatment? Furthermore, does the ‘expansive’ interpretation of the prohibition of torture or CIDTP encroach into the protective territory of the right to freedom of thought in this context?

This chapter identifies two commonalities between these rights: the first being their shared site of protection as the forum internum; the second being their shared normative underpinnings of dignity, integrity and autonomy. Identifying this common basis might help develop principled guidance on the permissibility of pain-free but coercive and interrogational use of neurotechnology. The chapter provides a contextual overview of the relevant scholarly developments related to the questions set out above. It examines the distinguishing features of the prohibition of torture or CIDTP as they relate to the protection of the mind and brain (the relevant case law does not refer to the concept of the forum internum), and the right to freedom of thought’s absolute protection of the forum internum before exploring how the commonality between these two rights guides the legal position on the coercive and interrogational use of neurotechnology (whether painful or not).

In approaching the human rights protection of the mind in an integrated way, this chapter interrogates the conceptual, normative and doctrinal webs between the right to freedom of thought and the prohibition of torture or CIDTP. The contribution to the literature offered here is, firstly, to call to attention the normative and instrumental relationship between these two rights which the chapter interrogates in the context of the coercive and interrogational use of neurotechnology. Secondly, although the prohibition of torture or CIDTP under some treaties would prohibit the coercive and interrogational use of neurotechnology (despite the absence of pain), this chapter questions whether such protection may be more appropriately sought under the right to freedom of thought. On this second aspect, whilst acknowledging that all rights are interrelated, interdependent, and indivisible, clarity on the delineation between these rights would help develop the latent right to freedom of thought.

title: Spatial Variation of Soil Radon and Thoron Exhalation Rates in Mineral-Enriched Beach Sands along the Chennai Megacity Coast, India
affiliations: , , , , , Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research, Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research,  and Sathyabama University

detail.title: Spatial Variation of Soil Radon and Thoron Exhalation Rates in Mineral-Enriched Beach Sands along the Chennai Megacity Coast, India
detail.abstract: The short-lived progenies of radon, thoron (220Rn), and radon (222Rn) are major global sources of ionizing radiation exposure and require continuous environmental monitoring because of their inhalation-related health risks. This study investigated the spatial distribution of soil-gas radon and thoron, their mass and surface exhalation rates, and the mineralogical controls on beach sands along the Chennai megacity coast in Southeast India. Twenty-four intertidal soil samples were analyzed using a RAD7 radon–thoron monitor (Durridge Co., USA), an electrostatic solid-state alpha detector optimized for thoron measurements. Radon mass exhalation rates ranged from 2 to 12 mBq/kg/h (mean: 2.42 mBq/kg/h), whereas thoron surface exhalation rates varied widely from 162 to 31,623 Bq/m2/h (mean: 3,688.08 Bq/m2/h). The highest soil-gas radon levels (4.5–12 Bq/m3) were observed in Kokkilamedu, a placer-rich zone. Exhalation rates were inversely related to grain size, with finer sediments releasing more radon and thoron than coarser sediments. However, higher heavy-mineral content, greater bulk density, and finer grain fractions also restricted exhalation, indicating strong mineralogical and textural control of radionuclide mobility. The sediments contained up to 12.5% heavy minerals, including ilmenite, zircon, and monazite, contributing to gamma radiation levels of up to 7.5 µR/h. The annual effective radon doses ranged from 0.12 to 0.45 mSv/y, remaining below the global safety limits. Elevated thoron exhalation in monazite-rich areas highlights the need for regular radiological surveillance, particularly among placer-deposit workers. These results provide baseline data on coastal sediment radiology and provenance to support environmental risk management and public health planning in the Chennai coastal zone.

title: Credit Where It's Not Due: Misbenchmarking by Active Bond Funds
affiliations: Villanova University - Department of Finance, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, University of Missouri at Columbia - Department of Finance and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Credit Where It's Not Due: Misbenchmarking by Active Bond Funds
detail.abstract: Misspecified benchmarks are prevalent among active bond mutual funds, due in part to the industry's overreliance on the Bloomberg U.S. Aggregate Index. Active funds outperform their self-declared benchmarks by 3% over 36 months, but this outperformance is entirely driven by the selection of benchmarks with mismatched systematic risks. When matched to a more appropriate benchmark based on return correlations, funds underperform. Benchmark-adjusted returns drive future flows, providing incentives for managers to misbenchmark. While benchmark changes are infrequent, they are strategic: funds switch to easier-to-beat benchmarks following a period of underperformance and subsequently experience a short-term increase in flows.

title: Is Economic Policy Uncertainty a Driver of Cryptocurrency Market Volatility?
affiliations: and Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) - Graduate School of Culture Technology

detail.title: Is Economic Policy Uncertainty a Driver of Cryptocurrency Market Volatility?
detail.abstract: The cryptocurrency market is sensitive to regulations and policy shifts, yet the dynamics of this relationship remain underexplored. This study investigates volatility spillover dynamics between G7 Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) indices and cryptocurrencies using a Time-Varying Parameter Vector Autoregression (TVP-VAR) model, which captures evolving relationships over time. The dataset comprises EPU indices from G7 countries, the PPP-weighted Global EPU, and the monthly average prices of 18 cryptocurrencies, including the stablecoin Tether(USDT), spanning May 2016 to October 2023. Our findings reveal that overall volatility spillover connectedness remains stable throughout the observed period, while EPU indices do not significantly transmit volatility to the cryptocurrency market. Interestingly, a few smaller-capital cryptocurrencies transmit volatility to EPU indices, whereas the stablecoin Tether (USDT) receives the highest spillovers. Results suggest the cryptocurrency market has matured and become less reactive to policy shifts, instead transmitting volatility to EPU indices.

title: Import Tariffs and the Systematic Response of Monetary Policy
affiliations: and

detail.title: Import Tariffs and the Systematic Response of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract: We estimate the macroeconomic effects of U.S. import tariff shocks using several tariff measurement and identification approaches. Tariff shocks reduce output but increase consumer prices. Monetary policy partially accommodates these shocks with a policy easing. To quantify the dependence on systematic monetary policy, we use empirically identified monetary policy shocks to construct counterfactuals that are robust against model misspecification and the Lucas critique. When monetary policy strictly stabilizes inflation, the output contraction at the trough is 36% larger than in the baseline. In contrast, strict output stabilization implies a peak inflation effect that almost doubles, compared to the baseline.

title: Life-Cycle Effects of Comprehensive Sex Education
affiliations: University of Southern Denmark - Interdisciplinary Centre for Population Dynamics and Lund University

detail.title: Life-Cycle Effects of Comprehensive Sex Education
detail.abstract: Using the introduction of comprehensive sex education in Sweden as a natural experiment, we explore how educational curricula can shape social norms and impact personal well-being. Inspired by liberal values, the curriculum taught more than just biology. It instilled lessons on abstinence, rational family planning, and the importance of taking social responsibility for personal decisions. We find that the reform successfully addressed its intended outcomes, reducing unwanted pregnancies, leading to fertility postponements and increasing female labor force participation. The findings suggest that social norms, internalized through school-based sex education, persistently affect people’s outcomes in significant ways.

title: Revisiting TFP Fluctuations: The Role of Goods-Market Search and Time Allocation

detail.title: Revisiting TFP Fluctuations: The Role of Goods-Market Search and Time Allocation
detail.abstract: Measured productivity fluctuates far more over the business cycle than technology. This paper shows that these movements mainly reflect coordination failures in the goods market. I develop a New Keynesian DSGE model, inspired by Barro's (2025) critique of frictionless goods markets, in which households allocate time between work and search, firms supply unmatched capacity, and trades form through goods-market search and matching. Matching efficiency determines capacity utilization and thus measured TFP. Bayesian estimation on U.S. and Euro Area data-using surveybased capacity utilization-shows that incorporating goods-market frictions sharply improves model fit and reduces the need for cost-push shocks. The interaction of sticky posted prices and flexible search prices generates a state-dependent demand elasticity, while the coordination channel links search effort to effective output: excess demand raises TFP by increasing match rates, excess supply lowers it by leaving capacity idle. The model identifies Barro-Grossman (1971) regimes in the data: the missing deflation after 2008 reflects a low-efficiency, classical-unemployment regime, whereas the post-COVID inflation surge arises from a high-tightness, repressed-inflation regime. Thus, short-run productivity is coordination-driven, and policy operates in a state-dependent environment where stabilizing market efficiency is as important as managing demand.

title: Cross-Border Acknowledgment IV: The Collapse of Domestic Remedies under EU Charter Article 47
affiliations: Semmelweis University

detail.title: Cross-Border Acknowledgment IV: The Collapse of Domestic Remedies under EU Charter Article 47
detail.abstract: Cross-Border Acknowledgment IV: The Collapse of Domestic Remedies under EU Charter Article 47 examines how, in the Semmelweis University case, every domestic effort to protect educational rights under EU law was superficial and ineffective. An international medical student was denied access to a compulsory anatomy practical, examined under invalid conditions, and faced threats of disciplinary actions for whistleblowing based on research. However, no Hungarian authority-whether the university, the Ombudsman, the NAIH data protection agency, the accreditation committee, or the administrative court-provided a prompt, justified, and effective response. This paper does not present new facts. Instead, it synthesizes and reinterprets existing evidence published in the author's SSRN series on Hungarian medical education and governance (Administrative Obstruction in EU Medical Education I, III, IV, VI; Cross-Border Acknowledgment of Academic Obstruction; Gatekeeper of Rights I-II; Educational Rights and Whistleblower Protection; Specimen Deficiency; Oral Exams Without Standards; Over-Enrolled and Under-Served). At the EU law level, it discusses Athanasiadou and Eliantonio's analysis of the "silence of the EU authorities" and the limits of legal oversight over administrative inaction, drawing parallels at the Member State level where institutions acknowledge complaints but allow Article 47 to become largely ineffective. In the higher education field, it examines the case against Pusztai et al.'s administrative-data study of Hungarian medical student attrition, arguing that administrative obstruction of access, assessment, and data governance likely contributes to the significantly higher dropout risk among self-financing international students. Cross-Border Acknowledgment IV therefore treats the Semmelweis dossier as a test case of systemic administrative failure within an EU Member State and contends that, under current legal and institutional arrangements, the only meaningful residual checks on such collapse are cross-border accreditation processes and EU rule-of-law monitoring.

title: Dynamic Bargaining under Ratchet Effects: Evidence from Cardiac Pacemakers
affiliations: Kyoto University and University of Tokyo - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Dynamic Bargaining under Ratchet Effects: Evidence from Cardiac Pacemakers
detail.abstract: This paper studies how Japan's ratchet-based medical device reimbursement rule distorts pricing incentives. Because reimbursement updates depend on transaction prices observed during designated sampling periods, hospitals and device sellers jointly raise prices when those periods occur, despite normally conflicting interests. Using a Nash-in-Nash bargaining model and transaction-level data, the study shows that hospitals possess greater bargaining power. Counterfactual simulations reveal that although the ratchet rule could have raised reimbursement prices substantially, its actual impact is small. This attenuated impact is attributable to institutional features of the reimbursement system: the government's use of a relatively long sampling window and its aggregation of products into broad functional categories.

title: Norming of IQ Tests on a Ratio Scale
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Norming of IQ Tests on a Ratio Scale

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there is no conflict of interest regarding the publication of this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a theoretical, mathematical and philosophical analysis and did not involve experiments with human participants or animals.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: In this article, we present a solution to one of the central problems of psychometrics over the past 100 years: a method for norming cognitive tests by producing scores on a ratio scale. This new approach is accompanied by many other complementary solutions, including the ability to accurately determine consistent values for the test ceilings, even when the theoretical rarity level at the top is much larger than the sample size. For example, in a sample of 3,000 subjects from a non-selective population, we can accurately determine the ceiling at the rarity level of 1 in 3 million by grouping the lower scores to compose a metric that allows us to estimate the higher scores while preserving the scale's internal consistency. The higher the ceiling and the more difficult it is to norm using traditional methods, the greater the benefits of this method. In a non-selective sample of 50,000 people, we can determine the ceiling down to the level of 1 in 1 billion. Alternatively, with a sample of only a few hundred people with significantly above-average IQs, heavily biased by self-selection, we were able to determine the ceiling down to the level of 1 in a few billion even without knowing the parameters of this sample's distribution. In samples severely contaminated by self-selection, we were able to neutralize this effect naturally, without the need for epicycle. We corrected for distortions in the dense tails and obtained a series of other advantages compared to traditional methods based on IRT and TCT [10], in addition to combining all the typical conceptual advantages inherent in ratio scales. We also opened the possibility of measuring animal and artificial intelligence on the same scale as human intelligence, among other possibilities yet to be discovered. We call this new procedure the "HM Method".

title: Small Language Models For Efficient Domain Data Retrieval Using Structured Query Language from Natural Language
affiliations: Hitachi Digital Services, Independent researcher, Independent researcher and Lecturer

detail.title: Small Language Models For Efficient Domain Data Retrieval Using Structured Query Language from Natural Language
detail.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are dominating AI landscapes due to their proven track of record in commercial and industrial deployments. Nevertheless, their rising voracious energy demands pose profound environmental and financial challenges. This study promotes the use of open-source small language models (SLMs) from Ollama, with parameters fewer than 5 billions, as viable, eco-conscious alternatives with built-in privacy optimality. Through automatic and manual behavioral comparison on Text-to-SQL information retrieval across four diverse datasets and 120 user-like questions, we evaluate 10 SLMs against a 120B-parameter model (gpt-oss-120b) to justify whether SLMs are capable of functioning as efficient as the large one. Results illuminate SLMs' prowess as qwen3:4b and gemma3:4b achieve SQL higher validity rates than gpt-oss-120b with high similarity scores. Natural language responses, validated via LLM-as-judge and human scrutiny, exhibit factual coherence and enhanced interpretability. Critically, SLMs slash inference latency (20-190s/query) and emissions (9.5-73 gCO2), enabling local deployment on consumer hardware for uncompromised privacy. This champions SLM-centric architectures for future agentic retrieval systems, curbing LLM overuse, mitigating carbon footprints, and democratizing AI. Code for reproduction is stored at: github.com/TheQuantScientist/TextToSQL.

title: Benchmarking Risk and Capital in Banks
affiliations: Howden Group Holdings, Howden Group Holdings and Howden Group Holdings

detail.title: Benchmarking Risk and Capital in Banks
detail.abstract: Banks are legally required to disclose their risks and exposures-both underlying and projected-to clients, investors, and regulators through regulatory reporting. The medium for disseminating this information is a lengthy publication known as the Pillar 3 report, which is dedicated solely to reporting risk and capital. This report is published annually alongside other important public disclosures, such as financial results, annual reports, etc. However, not all banks have the appropriate levels of sophistication needed to carry out the substantive tasks of risk evaluation and reporting, which, among other things include data collection, risk calculations and publishing of the Pillar 3 report. While larger banks may afford to devote strong technical support and hefty resources to carry out such tasks, smaller banks may not. For this reason, it would help to have in place a method that would enable smaller banks to obtain estimates of their risks and capital numbers without having to rely on considerable resources and technical expertise. We outline here a capital estimation method founded on peer analysis and benchmarking, making use of relationships that seem to exist between the financials of a bank and certain of its risk attributes. The approach, which is principally statistical, offers a means for banks to quickly gage their risks and risk capital amounts using only basic and high-level financial information, such as asset size and revenue. It is noted that, while such methods are commonly used in company rating practices and valuation of equity and other assets, they seem to be particularly absent in the fields of risk and capital management.

title: On the Use of Machine Learning Methods to Estimate Triangular Two-Level Panel Data Models with Individual Fixed Effects
affiliations: University of Geneva

detail.title: On the Use of Machine Learning Methods to Estimate Triangular Two-Level Panel Data Models with Individual Fixed Effects
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the use of machine learning to estimate triangular simultaneous equation models for panel data with an additive separable individual specific effect, and an additive separable disturbance term. First, we consider a model composed of a linear structural equation with one endogenous variable. The endogenous variable presents a nonlinear relationship with the instrumental variables and the exogenous regressors. The parameter of interest is the structural parameter of the endogenous variable. The identification of this parameter is obtained under the assumption of available exclusion restrictions and using a control function approach. The estimation of the parameter of interest is done using two proposed estimators composed of two steps. In the first step, we estimate the nonlinear reduced form equation using random forests and obtain the residuals. In the second step, we use the residuals as an estimated control function for the endogeneity in the structural equation. Later, we relax the functional form assumption in the structural equation and consider a semiparametric structural equation. In this new setting, we use random forests to estimate the nonparametric component of the structural equation. We use a Monte Carlo simulation to test the performance of the estimators proposed. We conclude that the estimators perform well, provided that we can learn accurately the nuisance parameter accurately in the first stage.
